query: As-cast HfMoTaTiZr has high strength at room temperature and elevated temperature but a relatively high density of 10.21 g cm−3. What single intervention could reduce its density without sacrificing its mechanical properties at room temperature and at elevated temperatures, including approximately 1000 °C? State the proposed intervention and mechanism, predict directional changes relative to as-cast HfMoTaTiZr, define the applicable temperature and loading boundaries, identify supporting prior evidence, and propose an experiment and rejection criterion that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Partial substitution of Hf by a controlled amount (~25–30 atomic % of the Hf content) with aluminum in the as‐cast HfMoTaTiZr alloy will lower its overall density by roughly 10–15% while preserving (or even modestly enhancing) its room‐temperature and ~1000 °C strength and ductility. This works because reducing the heavy Hf fraction decreases the average atomic weight and promotes additional lattice distortion strengthening via the solute effect, while keeping the single BCC solid‐solution structure intact.
generation.material_initial_state: As‐cast equiatomic HfMoTaTiZr, exhibiting a single-phase BCC solid solution with density ~10.21 g/cm³ and high yield strength at RT and elevated temperatures.
generation.intervention: Replace approximately 25–30% of the Hf atoms with Al (i.e. design an alloy Hf_(1−x)Al_xMoTaTiZr with x ~0.25–0.30).
generation.conditions: Mechanical testing under quasi-static loading at room temperature and at elevated temperatures (focusing on ~1000 °C), with microstructural characterization performed in the as‐cast state.
generation.structural_mediator: A maintained single BCC solid-solution phase with fine, homogeneous grain structure that supports both high yield strength and ductility.
generation.mechanism: Lightweight Al addition reduces the overall alloy density while its incorporation into the BCC matrix increases lattice distortion and solid-solution strengthening. The partial substitution minimizes the adverse effect on ductility that sometimes accompanies aggressive alloying, because the modest Al level helps to refine the microstructure without inducing deleterious intermetallics or excessive phase segregation.
generation.predicted_outcome: The modified alloy is expected to show a density reduction (targeting around 8.7–9.2 g/cm³) and mechanical properties (yield strength and ductility) at room temperature and ~1000 °C similar to those of the original HfMoTaTiZr alloy. A modest improvement or at least retention of the yield strength (within ±10%) and ductility is anticipated.
generation.baseline: The as‐cast HfMoTaTiZr alloy with high strength at room and elevated temperatures but a high density of approximately 10.21 g/cm³.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies to the as‐cast alloy state (no additional thermomechanical processing) and is valid for testing regimes up to approximately 1000 °C under quasi-static mechanical loading.
generation.uncertainty: This proposal combines the MD simulation findings (as in PMC10254787::web::012::3_1_effects_of_hf_and_ta_contents) indicating that reducing Hf content can increase strength, and prior experimental studies on light-element (Al) additions in similar RHEA systems (PMC8746096::web::002::1_introduction and PMC8074761::web::016::4_conclusions) that report density reduction and specific strength improvements. What is new here is the systematic experimental validation in the strictly as‐cast HfMoTaTiZr system at elevated temperatures, and clarifying the optimum substitution fraction that avoids loss of ductility—a point that has remained uncertain due to reported trade-offs in other studies.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of as‐cast Hf_(1−x)Al_xMoTaTiZr alloys with x varying from 0 (the as‐cast baseline) to 0.35. Characterize density, phase structure (via XRD and microscopy), and mechanical properties (yield strength and ductility) at room temperature and ~1000 °C via standard tensile or compressive tests.
measurements: XRD analysis to confirm single BCC phase
Room-temperature and high-temperature (≈1000 °C) compressive/tensile stress–strain curves to extract yield strength, ultimate strength, and plastic strain
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Al-substituted alloy either (a) exhibits a density reduction without maintaining yield strength within ±10% of the baseline at both RT and 1000 °C, or (b) shows a significant degradation in ductility (e.g., >20% reduction of plastic strain relative to the baseline), then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Based on the existing simulation results, this paper reduces the atomic content of Ta and Hf at the same time to investigate their effects on the mechanical properties of the HEA, the tensile stress–strain curve obtained from the simulation is shown in Figure 4d. On the other hand, to further verify the accuracy of the simulation results, as-cast HfxNbTaxTiZr HEA samples (x = 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1) were prepared and tested to compare with the simulation results. The tensile stress–strain curve obtained from the test is shown in Figure 4e. The tensile yield strengths of HEAs with different compositions were calculated based on the simulation curves and compared with the tensile strengths obtained by testing. The comparison results are shown in Figure 4f. It can be seen from the comparison results that the variation trend of the simulated values is in line with the actual test results. The variation trend of dislocation density shown in Figure 5 also provides evidence.

The subtraction of Ta from HfMoNbTaTiZr gives HfMoNbTiZr. At room temperature, the yield strength of alloy was 1351 MPa, and the ultimate strength was 1698 MPa when the strain was 17%. This alloy performs with better toughness than HfMoNbTaTiZr and HfMoTaTiZr does at room temperature. At 800 °C, the yield strength was 829 MPa and the ultimate strength was 1244 MPa when the strain was 18%. At 1000 °C, yield strength was 721 MPa, and the strength kept decreasing when the strain increased. At 1200 °C, the yield strength was 301 MPa. The strength of the alloy was almost constant after the yield point to the end of the test. The strain softening effect was balanced by the strengthening effect.

In this study, Co and Ni elements were added into Al0.8NbTiV alloy, which shows the best combination of strength and plasticity among a series of the single-phase AlxNbTiV alloys. To develop the precipitation-hardened light-weight RHEAs, the microstructure and mechanical properties have been systematically investigated for the presented newly designed RHEAs, as listed below: The AlxNbTiV (X = 0, 0.4, 0.8, 1) alloys in as-cast condition have single body-centered-cubic (BCC) structure. As the Al content increases up to 0.8, the yield strength is gradually enhanced to 1142 MPa without apparent reduction of the plasticity. Thus, the Al0.8NbTiV RHEA was selected for designing new precipitation-hardened light-weight RHEAs by addition of minor Co and Ni elements. The as-cast Al0.8NbTiVM0.2 (M = Co, Ni) alloys contain a single BCC phase. The yield strength of the as-cast Al0.8NbTiVM0.2 (M = Co, Ni) alloys at room temperature is higher than the Al0.8NbTiV alloy, which is due to the smaller atomic radius of Co and Ni in comparison with the atomic radii of other principal elements of the alloys, leading to significant solid-solution strengthening by severe lattice distortion.

Adding lightweight elements into RHEAs can effectively reduce the density and improve the specific strength [,,,]. For example, Senkov et al. fabricated Al0.4Hf0.6NbTaTiZr RHEA by adding Al into the HfNbTaTiZr RHEA. The density of the alloy decreased from 9.94 to 9.05 g/cm3, and the specific yield strength increased from 93.56 to 203.43 MPa∙cm3/g []. However, their plasticity deteriorated significantly. Recently, Yang et al. found that NbTiVTaAl0.25 RHEA with Al addition still have outstanding compressive plasticity greater than 50% []. Nevertheless, the specific strength of this alloy is only 151.48 MPa∙cm3/g, which has the potential for further improvement. In this work, a series of lightweight TaNbVTi-based RHEAs were fabricated by mechanical alloying (MA) followed by spark plasma sintering (SPS). The microstructural evolution and its effects on mechanical properties were analyzed.
